Triangle angle sum: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. Triangles are classified by angles (acute, right, obtuse, equiangular) and by sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral). In a right triangle the two acute angles are complementary. An exterior angle is formed by extending one side, and the Exterior Angle Theorem says it equals the sum of the two remote (non-adjacent) interior angles.
Congruent triangles SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS: Two triangles are congruent if all corresponding sides and angles are congruent. You can prove it with fewer facts: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them), AAS (two angles and a side not between them), and HL for right triangles (hypotenuse and a leg). SSA and AAA do not work. Once triangles are congruent, all their other corresponding parts are congruent (CPCTC).
Isosceles and equilateral triangles: In an isosceles triangle the two equal sides are the legs and the third side is the base. The Isosceles Triangle Theorem says the base angles (opposite the equal sides) are congruent, and its converse says that if two angles are congruent then the sides opposite them are congruent. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60 degree angles. In an isosceles triangle the bisector of the vertex angle is also the median and altitude to the base.
Medians, altitudes and bisectors: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, an altitude is a perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line of the opposite side, a perpendicular bisector cuts a side in half at 90 degrees and an angle bisector splits an angle. These lines meet at special points: the medians at the centroid (the balance point, two thirds of the way from each vertex), the perpendicular bisectors at the circumcenter (equally far from the vertices), the angle bisectors at the incenter (equally far from the sides) and the altitudes at the orthocenter.
Triangle inequality: The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side. So three lengths form a triangle only if the two shorter lengths add up to more than the longest. If two sides are a and b, the third side c must satisfy |a - b| < c < a + b. In a triangle the longest side is opposite the largest angle and the shortest side is opposite the smallest angle.
